```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
library(splines)        # ns(); ships with R, like MASS
library(glmnet)
library(rpart)
library(randomForest)
library(nnet)           # one-hidden-layer networks; ships with R, like MASS and splines
library(gapminder)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))
options(knitr.table.format = "html")
options(digits = 5)
# Base-graphics trees: small margins and labels allowed to use them, in every chunk.
knitr::opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), xpd = NA)
set.seed(5)
# Palette: viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second one.
v_dark <- "#440154"; v_blue <- "#31688e"; v_teal <- "#21918c"; v_green <- "#5ec962"
m_pink <- "#b73779"; m_purple <- "#8c2981"; m_orange <- "#fc8961"
mse <- function(y, pred) mean((y - pred)^2)
se_loss <- function(y, pred) sd((y - pred)^2) / sqrt(length(y))
# k-NN regression with several standardized inputs: squared distances by matrix algebra, then
# the mean outcome of the k nearest training rows. Week 1's knn_predict had one input.
knn_predict <- function(Xnew, Xtrain, ytrain, k) {
  d2 <- outer(rowSums(Xnew^2), rowSums(Xtrain^2), "+") - 2 * Xnew %*% t(Xtrain)
  apply(d2, 1, function(d) mean(ytrain[order(d)[1:k]]))
}
# The week's task: Spotify tracks (data note: data/spotify.md), one row per track, split three
# ways with the seminar's seed: 5,000 training, 2,000 selection, 3,000 test tracks.
sp <- read_csv("../../../files/spotify_tracks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000, genre = factor(playlist_genre))
feat <- c("danceability", "energy", "loudness", "speechiness", "acousticness",
          "instrumentalness", "liveness", "valence", "tempo", "duration_min", "release_year")
set.seed(5)
sp_id <- sample(nrow(sp))
sp_train <- sp[sp_id[1:5000], ]
sp_sel   <- sp[sp_id[5001:7000], ]
sp_test  <- sp[sp_id[7001:10000], ]
# Week 1's countries, 2007, for every one-input picture (a curve is visible with 142 points;
# Spotify's one-input relations are too weak to draw a basis with). GDP per capita unlogged, so
# that the relation is curved.
gm <- gapminder |> filter(year == 2007)
gm_grid <- tibble(gdpPercap = seq(min(gm$gdpPercap), max(gm$gdpPercap), length.out = 300))
# Coefficient paths from a glmnet fit as a labeled ggplot: minus log lambda on the horizontal
# axis (large lambda on the left), the named columns in color and labeled at the right.
path_plot <- function(fit, highlight, title) {
  B <- as.matrix(coef(fit))[-1, ]
  paths <- as_tibble(t(B)) |> mutate(loglam = -log(fit$lambda)) |>
    pivot_longer(-loglam, names_to = "variable", values_to = "coef") |>
    mutate(named = variable %in% highlight)
  # Labels at the right end, pushed apart vertically when two would overlap.
  lab <- paths |> filter(loglam == max(loglam), named) |> arrange(coef)
  gap <- 0.08 * diff(range(paths$coef)); y_lab <- lab$coef
  for (i in seq_along(y_lab)[-1]) y_lab[i] <- max(y_lab[i], y_lab[i - 1] + gap)
  lab$y_lab <- y_lab - (mean(y_lab) - mean(lab$coef))
  ggplot(paths, aes(loglam, coef, group = variable)) +
    geom_line(aes(colour = named), linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = v_blue), guide = "none") +
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(y = y_lab, label = variable), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.9, colour = v_dark) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(min(paths$loglam), max(paths$loglam) + 0.45 * diff(range(paths$loglam)))) +
    labs(x = expression(-log(lambda) ~ "(large" ~ lambda ~ "on the left)"), y = "coefficient", title = title) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
}
# The Spotify design with genre as dummies, standardized, for the penalized fits.
sp_X <- function(d) model.matrix(reformulate(c(feat, "genre"), "track_popularity"), d)[, -1]
sp_mu <- colMeans(sp_X(sp_train)); sp_sd <- apply(sp_X(sp_train), 2, sd)
sp_Xtr <- scale(sp_X(sp_train), sp_mu, sp_sd); sp_Xse <- scale(sp_X(sp_sel), sp_mu, sp_sd)
colnames(sp_Xtr) <- colnames(sp_Xse) <- sub("^genre", "genre: ", colnames(sp_X(sp_train)))
```

## Where week 4 left it {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
One minute. Last week how a model is fitted; this week what shapes a model can have. Each family briefly; each gets its own detail later.
:::

Last week: optimization, the general concepts and the methods that fit a model

This week: a few specific families of supervised models, each with its own **functional structure**, each introduced briefly. Every one of them gets more detail in a later week

Each family is a bet on the shape of $f^\star$. To compare the bets we need one task and one protocol

## The task: 10,000 Spotify tracks

::: {.notes}
Data note: data/spotify. Popularity is Spotify's score in January 2020, so recency is in it; the tenth at zero are tracks nobody plays. Ten audio features, the release year, a genre, squared loss. The plots use the 5,000 training tracks only: nothing from the other 5,000 is looked at before the split. Nothing is fitted yet.
:::

Predict a track's **popularity** (Spotify's score, 0 to 100) from ten audio features (danceability, energy, loudness, valence, tempo, ...), its release year and its genre. Loss: squared error

```{r}
#| label: spotify-task
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 12
p_hist <- ggplot(sp_train, aes(track_popularity)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = v_blue) +
  labs(x = "popularity", y = "tracks")
p_loud <- ggplot(sp_train, aes(loudness, track_popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.7, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-25, 0)) +
  labs(x = "loudness (dB)", y = "popularity")
p_year <- ggplot(sp_train, aes(release_year, track_popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.7, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "release year", y = NULL)
p_hist + p_loud + p_year
```

10,000 tracks from playlists of six genres ([data note](https://ml4ds.com/data/spotify.html)); the 5,000 training tracks plotted. Their popularity has variance `r round(var(sp_train$track_popularity))`: the MSE of predicting the mean for everyone

## Three kinds of data, one rule each

::: {.notes}
The protocol in a table; "selection set" is the course's name, books and software say validation set. Not said today: the selection winner's score is itself optimistic (a selected minimum); that is the seminar's problem 1 and week 7's topic. The third row is the one people break. ESL's word: the vault.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
| | Used for | How often |
|---|---|---|
| **Training** | fitting | as much as you like |
| **Selection** (books: validation) | choosing among fits: a method, its knob | as much as you like |
| **Test**, reserved | one number for the model you chose, with its standard error | **once** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,40,36]"}
:::

ESL's word for the third: a **vault**. Split once, at random, before looking (today 5,000, 2,000 and 3,000 tracks); refit the chosen model on training plus selection; open the vault once. A test set may score several competitors fixed in advance; nothing is chosen on it

::: {.retrieval}
Week 1's one rule, now for evaluation data: a row is fair game for scoring only if nothing about the model was chosen on it.
:::

## CTF competition: the baselines {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
What we can fit so far, scored on the selection tracks, both on the same eleven numeric inputs (genre is a factor and joins in the seminar, where the distance on its dummies is the students' decision): the mean 581, least squares 541, k-NN 528 at k = 100 chosen on the selection rows, standardized inputs. About one standard error apart: neither is far from the other. The question for the rest of the lecture: can a different shape beat both? The test set stays shut until the seminar.
:::

What we can fit so far, each a bet on $f^\star$: **least squares**, a plane (every input a slope); **logistic regression**, a plane for the log-odds (for a label, not today); **$k$ nearest neighbors**, a local average, its $k$ the knob

```{r}
#| label: baselines
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-width: 9.5
stdz <- function(d, mu, s) sweep(sweep(as.matrix(d[, feat]), 2, mu), 2, s, "/")
mu_f <- colMeans(sp_train[, feat]); sd_f <- apply(sp_train[, feat], 2, sd)
X_tr <- stdz(sp_train, mu_f, sd_f); X_se <- stdz(sp_sel, mu_f, sd_f)
f_lin <- reformulate(feat, "track_popularity")   # the eleven numeric inputs; genre joins in the seminar
fit_ls <- lm(f_lin, sp_train)
ks_sp <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200)
knn_sel <- sapply(ks_sp, function(k) mse(sp_sel$track_popularity, knn_predict(X_se, X_tr, sp_train$track_popularity, k)))
k_sp <- ks_sp[which.min(knn_sel)]
preds <- list(
  "baseline: the training mean" = rep(mean(sp_train$track_popularity), nrow(sp_sel)),
  "least squares on the 11 numeric inputs" = predict(fit_ls, sp_sel),
  "k nearest neighbors on the same 11, k chosen here" = knn_predict(X_se, X_tr, sp_train$track_popularity, k_sp))
lb <- imap_dfr(preds, ~ tibble(competitor = .y, mse = mse(sp_sel$track_popularity, .x),
                                se = se_loss(sp_sel$track_popularity, .x))) |>
  mutate(competitor = fct_reorder(competitor, -mse))
ggplot(lb, aes(mse, competitor)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = mse - se, xmax = mse + se), width = 0.25, colour = "grey60", orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 4, colour = v_dark) +
  labs(x = "MSE on the 2,000 selection tracks", y = NULL, caption = "bars: one standard error")
```

The local average ($k = `r k_sp`$) and the plane, one standard error apart. Can a different shape beat both? The test set stays shut

## The plan: several structures, each tuned

::: {.notes}
The task for the rest of the lecture, said once. Each family is a shape; each has a knob that sets how far the shape may bend to the data; the knob is chosen on the selection tracks, so that what gets compared is the best version of each kind. The knobs are named here and met one by one.
:::

Try several types of model, each with a different functional structure for $f$:

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| Structure | Family | The knob |
|---|---|---|
| a plane, shrunk or sparse | ridge, lasso | $\lambda$, how hard the penalty pulls |
| a sum of one-input curves | additive splines | $J$, how many basis functions per input |
| rectangles with a constant in each | a tree | its depth |
| an average of many trees | a random forest | (defaults today) |
| a composition: a GLM of GLMs | a neural network | $M$, how many hidden units |

: {tbl-colwidths="[36,26,38]"}
:::

and **tune each model so that it is the best version of its kind**: every knob chosen on the selection tracks, as $k$ was. Then compare the best of each kind

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a penalty is a knob written into the objective. Two penalties, two bets.
:::

### Part 2: ridge and lasso

## Regularized (i.e. penalized) regression

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide; its James--Stein opening is week 7's one slide, so the motivation here is week 4's early stopping. "Loss plus penalty" is the shape of most of today's methods.
:::

Motivation: week 4 stopped gradient descent early, and the number of steps became a knob that controlled how far the fit went. Can the knob be written into the objective instead?

. . .

For some penalty function $\mathcal P_\lambda$, which depends on a tuning parameter $\lambda$, the estimator

$$\hat \beta_\lambda = \arg \min_\beta \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta)$$
is "regularized" or shrunk (shranken?) toward values that decrease the penalty. Often $\mathcal P_\lambda = \lambda \| \cdot \|$ for some norm

. . .

Many ML methods are optimizing "loss + penalty"

## Ridge (i.e. L2 penalized) regression

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, whole. This lambda is the course's lambda: the objective with the squared error not divided by n. glmnet divides the squared error by n and the ridge penalty by 2, so its lambda is this one over n up to that factor; the path figures' axes are glmnet's. Conventions, said once: the intercept is not penalized, and the columns are standardized before the penalty is applied (glmnet's default), since a penalty on beta_j depends on the units of x_j.
:::

- Originally motivated by problems where $\mathbf X^T \mathbf X$ is uninvertible (or badly conditioned, i.e. almost uninvertible)

- If $p > n$ then this always happens

- Least squares estimator is undefined or numerically unstable

For some constant $\lambda > 0$,
$$\text{minimize } \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2$$
**Shrinks** coefficients $\hat \beta$ toward 0

Larger coefficients are penalized more (squared penalty)

## What $\lambda$ controls {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Exercise 2 derives the equations: the gradient of the penalized objective. Invertible for every positive lambda because X'X is positive semidefinite and lambda I adds lambda to every eigenvalue; that is "fitting when p > n". The figure: ridge on the Spotify training tracks, the eleven numeric inputs and five genre dummies, standardized; minus log lambda on glmnet's scale, so large lambda is on the left, every coefficient near zero; lambda to zero on the right, least squares (p = 16 < n here). Energy, duration and the pop and rap genres carry the largest coefficients.
:::

```{r}
#| label: spotify-paths
#| include: false
# Ridge and lasso paths on the Spotify training tracks: the eleven numeric inputs and five genre
# dummies, standardized (glmnet's default standardization is turned off because the columns are).
ridge_sp <- glmnet(sp_Xtr, sp_train$track_popularity, alpha = 0, standardize = FALSE)
lasso_sp <- glmnet(sp_Xtr, sp_train$track_popularity, alpha = 1, standardize = FALSE)
B_l <- as.matrix(coef(lasso_sp))[-1, ]
first_in <- names(sort(apply(B_l, 1, function(b) min(which(b != 0)))))[1:6]   # the first six to enter the lasso path
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Set the gradient of $\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2$ to zero (exercise 2):
$$
(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)\,\hat\beta_\lambda = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y
$$
$$
\hat\beta_\lambda = (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y
$$

$\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I$ is invertible for every $\lambda > 0$, whatever $n$ and $p$: one solution even when $p > n$

$\lambda \to 0$: least squares (when it exists). $\lambda \to \infty$: $\hat\beta_\lambda \to \mathbf 0$
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: ridge-path
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| out-width: "100%"
path_plot(ridge_sp, first_in, "ridge on the Spotify training tracks")
```
$\hat\beta_\lambda$ against $-\log\lambda$: the 16 standardized inputs (eleven numeric, five genre dummies), six named
:::
:::

## Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, whole. Two forms; that they give the same family of solutions is a KKT fact and is not today's. The 1/2n is glmnet's scaling; the ridge slide did not divide by n.
:::

A simple `diff` to remember lasso/ridge is via the penalty/constraint (1-norm instead of 2-norm). Lasso is

$$\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n}\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 \text{ s. t. } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t$$
where $\| \beta \|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|$. Lagrangian form

$$\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n} \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_1$$

## Lasso vs ridge: solution paths of $\hat \beta$

::: {.notes}
The legacy figure's two panels, on the Spotify training tracks instead of the legacy simulation. Right panel, read left to right: at large lambda everything is zero, coefficients enter one at a time as lambda falls (energy and duration first, then instrumentalness and the pop genre), and several stay at exactly zero until far right. Left panel: every path shrinks toward zero and none sits at zero over an interval. Same inputs as the ridge slide.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: ridge-path-again
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "100%"
path_plot(ridge_sp, first_in, "ridge")
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: lasso-path
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "100%"
path_plot(lasso_sp, first_in, "lasso")
```
:::
:::

Spotify, the same 16 inputs, large $\lambda$ on the left. The lasso's coefficients are exactly zero over whole ranges of $\lambda$ and enter one at a time; ridge's are never zero. Why, and what the lasso does when $p > n$: week 7

### Part 3: additive models

## Three ways to estimate a curve {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Week 1's data and week 1's k-NN, GDP per capita unlogged so that the relation is curved. Three ideas, named once: average nearby (k-NN; a kernel weights by distance instead of cutting at k), fit a line nearby (loess with degree 1), fit a basis (the next two slides; week 7 adds its penalty). We focus on the third; the others are names. All three are curves, and all three have a knob.
:::

Week 1's data, life expectancy on GDP per capita, 142 countries (no log this time). Three ways to turn a line into a curve

```{r}
#| label: three-ways
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 12
knn_one <- function(x0, x, y, k) mean(y[order(abs(x - x0))[1:k]])
three <- bind_rows(
  tibble(gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = sapply(gm_grid$gdpPercap, knn_one, x = gm$gdpPercap, y = gm$lifeExp, k = 10),
         method = "average nearby: k = 10 nearest neighbors"),
  tibble(gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = predict(loess(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, gm, degree = 1), gm_grid),
         method = "fit a line nearby: loess"),
  tibble(gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = predict(lm(lifeExp ~ ns(gdpPercap, df = 4), gm), gm_grid),
         method = "fit a basis: natural spline, J = 4")) |>
  mutate(method = fct_inorder(method))
ggplot(gm, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = three, aes(y = fit, colour = method), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(v_teal, m_orange, v_dark)) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", strip.text = element_text(size = 14)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (dollars)", y = "life expectancy")
```

**Average nearby** ($k$-NN; a *kernel* weights by distance instead of cutting at $k$). **Fit a line nearby** (*loess*). **Fit a basis**: fixed curves, combined by least squares. We now focus on the third

## A spline is regression on basis functions

::: {.notes}
ns() is in the splines package, which ships with R. Polynomials 1, x, x squared are a basis too, each global; each spline basis function is local, and that is the point. Natural cubic spline: cubic pieces between knots, two continuous derivatives at each knot, linear beyond the end knots; knots at quantiles of x. lm adds the intercept.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: spline-basis
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "100%"
basis_mat <- ns(gm_grid$gdpPercap, df = 6)
tibble(gdpPercap = rep(gm_grid$gdpPercap, 6), b = as.vector(basis_mat),
       j = factor(rep(1:6, each = nrow(gm_grid)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(gdpPercap, b, colour = j)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (dollars)", y = NULL, colour = "j",
       title = "six natural-spline basis functions") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16), legend.position = "none")
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
A **basis**: fixed functions $b_1(x), \ldots, b_J(x)$ of one input, combined by least squares:
$$
f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j\, b_j(x)
$$
linear in $\beta$: `lm(lifeExp ~ ns(gdp, df = J))`, `ns()` building the $J$ columns

A **natural cubic spline**: cubic pieces joined smoothly at knots, linear beyond the ends. The basis functions are the bends the knots allow; `lm` adds $\beta_0$
:::
:::

## The basis size is the knob

::: {.notes}
Same data, J = 2, 5, 15. J small, nearly a line; J large, wiggles, and at J = n the curve passes through every point with training error zero. Which J: the selection set, as for k and lambda. Week 7 adds a penalty on wiggliness instead, and J becomes a ceiling.
:::

```{r}
#| label: basis-size
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 12
fits_J <- map_dfr(c(2, 5, 15), function(J) {
  fit_J <- predict(lm(lifeExp ~ ns(gdpPercap, df = J), gm), gm_grid)
  tibble(size = paste("J =", J), gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = fit_J)
}) |>
  mutate(size = fct_inorder(size))
ggplot(gm, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = fits_J, aes(y = fit), colour = v_dark, linewidth = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ size) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (dollars)", y = "life expectancy")
```

Small $J$: almost a line. Large $J$: the curve follows the points, and at $J = n$ it passes through every one (training error zero). Which $J$? The selection set, as for $k$ and $\lambda$. Week 7: a penalty on wiggliness instead, with $J$ as a ceiling

## Additive modeling assumption

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide. g is the link, identity today. One function per input, added up; a coefficient is the special case. Only the sum is determined, so each f_j is centered and the level sits in beta_0.
:::

- **Linearity** assumption: each predictor has a *coefficient*

$$g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 + \beta_2 \mathbf x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p \mathbf x_p$$

- **Additivity** assumption: each predictor has a *function*

$$g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + f_1( \mathbf x_1) + f_2( \mathbf x_2) + \cdots + f_p(\mathbf x_p)$$

Includes linear models as special case if $f_j(\mathbf x_j) = \beta_j \mathbf x_j$

Today each $f_j$ is a spline with $J$ basis functions, so the whole model is one least-squares fit on $pJ$ columns: `lm(y ~ ns(x1, J) + ns(x2, J) + ...)`. The GAM in the reading is this model, with a link

## An additive model for popularity

::: {.notes}
Spotify, the training tracks: six of the numeric inputs as splines with J = 4, genre as a factor, one least-squares fit on 30 columns. R squared about 0.17: most of popularity is not in these inputs, which is the honest state of affairs. Each panel is a fitted component, centered, over the middle 98 percent of its input. Read two: loudness (louder tracks score higher, 20 points across the range), release year (the oldest tracks score high, a low around 2012, then the steep rise into 2019 and 2020: recency, as the data note says). Energy falls once loudness is in the model: the two are correlated, and the component is what energy adds with loudness held fixed, week 2's reading. Backfitting, week 8, is how these components are found when the one-input fits are not least squares.
:::

```{r}
#| label: spotify-additive-fit
#| echo: true
fit_add <- lm(track_popularity ~ ns(loudness, 4) + ns(release_year, 4) +
                ns(danceability, 4) + ns(duration_min, 4) + ns(energy, 4) +
                ns(acousticness, 4) + genre, data = sp_train)
```

```{r}
#| label: spotify-components
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 12
add_vars <- c("loudness", "release_year", "danceability", "duration_min", "energy", "acousticness")
comp_grid <- function(v) {
  g <- sp_train[rep(1, 200), ]
  g[[v]] <- seq(quantile(sp_train[[v]], 0.01), quantile(sp_train[[v]], 0.99), length.out = 200)
  g
}
comp <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(add_vars), function(j) {
  g <- comp_grid(add_vars[j])
  tibble(input = add_vars[j], x = g[[add_vars[j]]], component = predict(fit_add, g, type = "terms")[, j])
})) |> mutate(input = fct_inorder(input))
ggplot(comp, aes(x, component)) +
  geom_line(colour = v_dark, linewidth = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ input, scales = "free_x", nrow = 2) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "component of popularity")
```

One fit, `r length(coef(fit_add))` coefficients, and a curve per input to read instead of a coefficient: what the model adds for that input with the others held fixed

Compress: a different shape altogether, rectangles with a constant in each; then why one tree is not enough and what averaging many does.

### Part 4: trees and forests

## Decision trees {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a sequence of yes-or-no questions, each about one input, is a model too.
:::

### Are you eligible for the COVID-19 vaccine?

- If `Age >= 50` then `yes`, otherwise continue
- If `HighRisk == TRUE` then `yes`, otherwise continue
- If `Job == CareWorker` then `yes`, otherwise `no`

This is (arguably) more interpretable than a linear model with multiple predictors

(Note: this is not the real vaccination criteria, but it was close to this in early 2021)

## A regression tree for popularity

::: {.notes}
The legacy penguin tree, on the Spotify training tracks: popularity on release year and energy (the first two inputs to enter the lasso path), depth 3, at least 250 tracks in a leaf. Read it from the top: one question per node, a number in each leaf. The 2018 cutoff splits first; energy matters on both sides, with different cutoffs. The leaf values are mean popularity in the leaf.
:::

```{r}
#| label: spotify-tree
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "96%"
fit_tree <- rpart(track_popularity ~ release_year + energy, sp_train,
                  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3, cp = 0, minbucket = 250))
plot(fit_tree, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1)
text(fit_tree, pretty = 0, cex = 1.9, digits = 3)
```

## Regression tree predictions

::: {.notes}
The same tree drawn in the input plane: each leaf is a rectangle, and the prediction is the mean popularity of the training tracks in it. A step function in two inputs, flat inside each rectangle: nothing smooth, nothing additive. The energy question is asked on both sides of 2018 with different cutoffs, which an additive model could not do.
:::

```{r}
#| label: spotify-rectangles
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "78%"
# The tree's prediction on a grid of the input plane: each leaf is a rectangle with one value.
leaf_grid <- expand_grid(release_year = seq(1957, 2020, by = 0.25), energy = seq(0, 1, by = 0.005)) |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(fit_tree, pick(everything())))
ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = leaf_grid, aes(release_year, energy, fill = predicted), alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(data = sp_train, aes(release_year, energy), colour = "white", alpha = 0.25, size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(end = 0.95, name = "predicted\npopularity") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "release year", y = "energy")
```

Each leaf is a rectangle with one value; the training tracks in white. The three narrow strips on the right are the leaves for 2018 and for 2019 to 2020, split again by energy

## One predictor, every cutoff

::: {.notes}
New slide, before the loop. One input, release year: for every cutoff, split the training tracks in two, predict each side's mean, and record the training MSE; the best cutoff is where the curve is lowest, 2018 here (the recency effect). The right panel is the two-leaf fit that cutoff gives: one question. Week 8 does this by hand and scores every cutoff in one pass.
:::

```{r}
#| label: best-cutoff
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 12
cuts <- sort(unique(sp_train$release_year)); cuts <- cuts[-1]
split_mse <- sapply(cuts, function(c) {
  left <- sp_train$release_year < c
  (sum((sp_train$track_popularity[left] - mean(sp_train$track_popularity[left]))^2) +
   sum((sp_train$track_popularity[!left] - mean(sp_train$track_popularity[!left]))^2)) / nrow(sp_train)
})
best_cut <- cuts[which.min(split_mse)]
left <- sp_train$release_year < best_cut
step_df <- tibble(x = c(min(sp_train$release_year), best_cut, best_cut, max(sp_train$release_year)),
                  y = c(rep(mean(sp_train$track_popularity[left]), 2), rep(mean(sp_train$track_popularity[!left]), 2)))
p_cut <- ggplot(tibble(cut = cuts, mse = split_mse), aes(cut, mse)) +
  geom_line(colour = v_blue, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = tibble(cut = best_cut, mse = min(split_mse)), colour = m_orange, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "cutoff on release year", y = "training MSE of the two-leaf fit", title = paste("every cutoff tried; the best is", best_cut)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
p_step <- ggplot(sp_train, aes(release_year, track_popularity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.7, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_path(data = step_df, aes(x, y), colour = m_orange, linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "release year", y = "popularity", title = "the best two-leaf fit: one question") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
p_cut + p_step
```

For one input: try every cutoff, predict each side's mean, keep the cutoff with the smallest training MSE. One question, two leaves

## Recursive rectangular splitting on predictors

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, now the loop around the last slide: every input, its best cutoff, the best of those; then the same on each side. Greedy. How deep to grow and how to prune back are week 8's; today a depth is the tree's knob, chosen like the others.
:::

"Stratification of the feature space"

```
Input: subset of data
  For each predictor variable x_j in subset
    Scan cutoff values to find the best split for x_j (last slide)
Output: the predictor and cutoff with the best improvement
```

. . .

Starting from the full dataset, compute the first split as above

**Recurse**: take the two subsets of data from each side of the split and plug them both back into the same function

Until some **stopping rule** prevents more splitting (today: a maximum depth, the tree's knob; growing deep and pruning back is week 8)

## A tree is unstable

::: {.notes}
New slide, before the fix. Gapminder, where 142 points make it visible: eight resamples of the countries (draws with replacement, the same size), a depth-3 tree and a J = 4 spline on each. The trees' cutoffs jump between resamples and their steps jump with them; the splines barely move. Across the grid the eight trees' predictions have an average standard deviation of about 1.6 years, the splines' about 0.9. A tree has high variance; the orange line, the average of the eight trees, is already smoother than any of them, which is the next slide.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tree-variance
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-width: 12
set.seed(3)
resamples <- map_dfr(1:8, function(b) {
  d <- slice_sample(gm, n = nrow(gm), replace = TRUE)
  t_b <- rpart(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, d, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3, cp = 0, minbucket = 5))
  s_b <- lm(lifeExp ~ ns(gdpPercap, df = 4), d)
  bind_rows(tibble(b = b, method = "a depth-3 tree", gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = predict(t_b, gm_grid)),
            tibble(b = b, method = "a natural spline, J = 4", gdpPercap = gm_grid$gdpPercap, fit = predict(s_b, gm_grid)))
})
tree_avg <- resamples |> filter(method == "a depth-3 tree") |>
  group_by(gdpPercap) |> summarize(fit = mean(fit)) |> mutate(method = "a depth-3 tree")
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = gm, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp), colour = "grey60", size = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = resamples, aes(gdpPercap, fit, group = b), colour = v_blue, alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = tree_avg, aes(gdpPercap, fit), colour = m_orange, linewidth = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(40, 85)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (dollars)", y = "life expectancy")
```

Week 1's countries, resampled eight times (blue, one fit per resample). The trees' cutoffs move with the sample and the steps move with them; the splines barely move. Orange: the average of the eight trees

## Random forests: many trees, one model

::: {.notes}
Said, not derived: a random forest grows hundreds of trees, each on a resample of the training rows (the last slide's draws with replacement) with a random subset of the inputs offered at each split, and averages them: the orange line, with hundreds of trees instead of eight. One model, smoother and more stable than any one tree, and no knob to tune today (the defaults). What the resampling and the random subsets do, how much averaging buys and what correlation costs: week 8.
:::

A **random forest** is a method that combines many trees into one model: it grows hundreds of trees, each on a resample of the training rows with a random subset of the inputs offered at each split, and averages their predictions

The last slide's orange line, with hundreds of trees instead of eight: one model, smoother and more stable than any one tree

Today: `randomForest()` with its defaults, no knob. How it works and why averaging helps: week 8

::: {.notes}
Compress: one more structure, built by composing what we have: a regression whose inputs are themselves regressions.
:::

### Part 5: neural networks

## A GLM of GLMs {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
The whole idea on one slide, by analogy with what students know. A GLM (week 3): a link applied to a linear predictor. Iterate: feed the inputs into M logistic regressions, take their outputs as new inputs, and run a linear regression (or a logistic one, for a label) on those. The hidden units are a basis like part 3's, except that the basis is fitted to the data rather than fixed in advance, and each basis function uses all the inputs at once. Iterate again and the network is deep. Symbols: M hidden units, w_k the k-th unit's weights, sigma the logistic function.
:::

```{r}
#| label: network-picture
#| include: false
# The one-hidden-layer picture: p inputs, M hidden units, one output.
nn_inputs <- tibble(x = 0, y = seq(3.2, -0.2, length.out = 4), lab = c("x[1]", "x[2]", "...", "x[p]"))
nn_hidden <- tibble(x = 1.6, y = seq(2.8, 0.2, length.out = 3), lab = c("h[1]", "h[2]", "h[M]"))
nn_out <- tibble(x = 3.2, y = 1.5, lab = "f(x)")
nn_e1 <- expand_grid(a = 1:4, b = 1:3) |> filter(a != 3) |>
  mutate(x = nn_inputs$x[a], y = nn_inputs$y[a], xend = nn_hidden$x[b], yend = nn_hidden$y[b])
nn_e2 <- tibble(x = nn_hidden$x, y = nn_hidden$y, xend = nn_out$x, yend = nn_out$y)
nn_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = nn_e1, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = v_blue, alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(data = nn_e2, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = m_pink, alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = filter(nn_inputs, lab != "..."), aes(x, y), size = 15, colour = "grey35", fill = "white", shape = 21, stroke = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = nn_hidden, aes(x, y), size = 17, colour = v_blue, fill = "#e8f0f7", shape = 21, stroke = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = nn_out, aes(x, y), size = 17, colour = m_pink, fill = "#fbe9f1", shape = 21, stroke = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = bind_rows(nn_inputs, nn_hidden, nn_out), aes(x, y, label = lab), parse = TRUE, size = 6.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 3.8, label = "inputs", size = 5.5, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.6, y = 3.8, label = "M hidden units", size = 5.5, colour = v_blue) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = 3.8, label = "output", size = 5.5, colour = m_pink) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.4, 3.6), ylim = c(-0.6, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()
```

Week 3's GLM: a link applied to a linear predictor. Now iterate it

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: network-diagram
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "100%"
nn_plot
```
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
Each **hidden unit** is a logistic regression of the inputs, with its own weights: $h_k(x) = \sigma(w_{k0} + w_k^T x)$, where $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$

The **output** is a linear regression on the hidden units (logistic, for a label): $f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^M \beta_k\, h_k(x)$

A GLM whose inputs are the outputs of $M$ GLMs. Iterate once more: a *deep* network
:::
:::

A basis like part 3's, except that the basis is fitted to the data along with the coefficients, and each $h_k$ uses every input at once

## What to know about networks today

::: {.notes}
Three things and no more. Represent: with enough hidden units a network can come as close as you like to any smooth f-star (stated in week 11; universal approximation); the price is M times (p + 1) weights that all have to be fitted. Fit: week 4's stochastic gradient descent on a loss with every feature of week 4's part 3 (not convex: the hilly road, the saddle). The knob: M, chosen on the selection tracks; depth, and the penalty on the weights, are later knobs. nnet() in R, which ships with the base install; week 11 and ST311 do the rest.
:::

**What it can represent.** With enough hidden units, a network can come as close as you like to any smooth $f^\star$ (stated, week 11). The price: $M(p + 1) + M + 1$ weights, all to be fitted from the data

**How it is fitted.** Week 4's stochastic gradient descent, on a loss with every feature of week 4's part 3: not one valley but many, with plateaus and saddles between them

**The knob.** $M$, the number of hidden units, chosen on the selection tracks like the others; depth and a penalty on the weights are later knobs. In R, `nnet(size = M)`

Today the network is one more structure in the comparison; how it is built and trained in depth is week 11's, and ST311's

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: five families, five bets; three truths, one protocol, and the training error of every one of them.
:::

### Part 6: which structure?

## Three truths, one protocol {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Ten inputs, uniform on minus one to one, noise sd 1, so the floor is an MSE of 1. The network: M chosen on the selection rows, a small fixed ridge penalty on its weights, fitted by nnet; with 300 rows it stays small. Truth A is a plane in three of the ten; B is three smooth one-input curves (f1 = -1 + 2x - x^2, f2 = sin(pi x), f3 = exp(-5(x - 1/2)^2)), scaled by 1.5, in three of the ten; C is one step that needs two inputs at once (signal variance 3, of which the best sum of one-input functions holds 2 and the product the last 1). Every knob chosen on the 100 selection rows, then the chosen fit refitted on the 400 training-plus-selection rows; the test set is 2,000 rows because the truth is simulated and we can afford it. Forest with its defaults, no knob. The ask: two minutes, a show of hands per truth; take the reasons, not only the names.
:::

$p = 10$ inputs, uniform on $[-1, 1]$; $y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon$, noise variance $\sigma^2 = 1$. Three truths, each using two or three inputs:

- **A, sparse linear:** $f^\star(x) = 2x_1 - 1.5x_2 + x_3$
- **B, additive smooth:** $f^\star(x) = 1.5\,[f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + f_3(x_3)]$, smooth $f_j$
- **C, one step, two inputs at once:** $f^\star(x) = 4 \cdot \mathbf 1\{x_1 > 0,\ x_2 > 0\}$

**One protocol.** 300 training, 100 selection, 2,000 test rows. Seven competitors: least squares; lasso ($\lambda$); $k$-NN ($k$); additive splines ($J$); a tree (depth); a forest; a network ($M$). Knobs chosen on the selection rows, the fit refitted on training plus selection, scored once

::: {.ask}
For each truth: which family wins, which loses, and why?
:::

```{r}
#| label: compare-families
#| include: false
# Every family fitted to one simulated dataset under the protocol above: each knob chosen on the
# selection rows, the chosen fit refitted on training plus selection (k-NN uses those rows as its
# neighbors), then scored on the test rows. Returns one row per competitor with training MSE (on
# the refit rows), test MSE and its standard error. wide = TRUE drops least squares and the
# additive fit (no unique fit with more columns than rows) and adds ridge.
compare_families <- function(truth, p, n_train, n_sel, n_test, seed, wide = FALSE) {
  set.seed(seed)
  gen <- function(n) {
    X <- matrix(runif(n * p, -1, 1), n, p); colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:p)
    tibble(as.data.frame(X), y = truth(X) + rnorm(n))
  }
  tr <- gen(n_train); se <- gen(n_sel); te <- gen(n_test); all <- bind_rows(tr, se)
  Xtr <- as.matrix(tr[, 1:p]); Xse <- as.matrix(se[, 1:p]); Xte <- as.matrix(te[, 1:p]); Xall <- as.matrix(all[, 1:p])
  score <- function(name, pred_all, pred_te)
    tibble(competitor = name, train = mse(all$y, pred_all), test = mse(te$y, pred_te), se = se_loss(te$y, pred_te))
  out <- list()
  if (!wide) {
    fit <- lm(y ~ ., all)
    out$ls <- score("least squares", fitted(fit), predict(fit, te))
  }
  las <- glmnet(Xtr, tr$y)
  lam <- las$lambda[which.min(apply(predict(las, Xse), 2, function(q) mse(se$y, q)))]
  las_all <- glmnet(Xall, all$y, lambda = lam)
  out$lasso <- score("lasso", predict(las_all, Xall), predict(las_all, Xte))
  if (wide) {
    rid <- glmnet(Xtr, tr$y, alpha = 0)
    lamr <- rid$lambda[which.min(apply(predict(rid, Xse), 2, function(q) mse(se$y, q)))]
    rid_all <- glmnet(Xall, all$y, alpha = 0, lambda = lamr)
    out$ridge <- score("ridge", predict(rid_all, Xall), predict(rid_all, Xte))
  }
  ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 30, 50)
  k <- ks[which.min(sapply(ks, function(k) mse(se$y, knn_predict(Xse, Xtr, tr$y, k))))]
  out$knn <- score("k-NN", knn_predict(Xall, Xall, all$y, k), knn_predict(Xte, Xall, all$y, k))
  if (!wide) {
    gam_f <- function(J) reformulate(sprintf("ns(x%d, df = %d)", 1:p, J), "y")
    Js <- c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8)
    J <- Js[which.min(sapply(Js, function(J) mse(se$y, predict(lm(gam_f(J), tr), se))))]
    g <- lm(gam_f(J), all)
    out$gam <- score("additive splines", fitted(g), predict(g, te))
  }
  ds <- 1:8
  d <- ds[which.min(sapply(ds, function(d) mse(se$y, predict(rpart(y ~ ., tr,
         control = rpart.control(maxdepth = d, cp = 0, minbucket = 5)), se))))]
  t <- rpart(y ~ ., all, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = d, cp = 0, minbucket = 5))
  out$tree <- score("tree", predict(t, all), predict(t, te))
  rf <- randomForest(y ~ ., all, ntree = 300)
  out$forest <- score("forest", predict(rf, all), predict(rf, te))
  # A one-hidden-layer network: M chosen on the selection rows, a small fixed penalty on the weights.
  Ms <- c(2, 4, 8, 16)
  nn_fit <- function(d, M) { set.seed(10); nnet(y ~ ., d, size = M, decay = 0.01, linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, MaxNWts = 5000, trace = FALSE) }
  M <- Ms[which.min(sapply(Ms, function(M) mse(se$y, predict(nn_fit(tr, M), se))))]
  nn <- nn_fit(all, M)
  out$network <- score("network", predict(nn, all), predict(nn, te))
  bind_rows(out) |> mutate(knob = paste0("lambda ", signif(lam, 2), ", k ", k, ", J ", if (wide) NA else J, ", depth ", d, ", M ", M))
}
# Truth B's three curves: a parabola, a sine, a bump (the legacy GAM deck's simulation).
f1 <- function(x) -1 + 2 * x - x^2
f2 <- function(x) sin(pi * x)
f3 <- function(x) exp(-5 * (x - 1/2)^2)
truth_A <- function(X) 2 * X[, 1] - 1.5 * X[, 2] + X[, 3]
truth_B <- function(X) 1.5 * (f1(X[, 1]) + f2(X[, 2]) + f3(X[, 3]))
truth_C <- function(X) 4 * (X[, 1] > 0 & X[, 2] > 0)
res_A  <- compare_families(truth_A, p = 10, 300, 100, 2000, seed = 1)
res_Aw <- compare_families(truth_A, p = 200, 100, 50, 2000, seed = 2, wide = TRUE)
res_B  <- compare_families(truth_B, p = 10, 300, 100, 2000, seed = 1)
res_C  <- compare_families(truth_C, p = 10, 300, 100, 2000, seed = 1)
leaderboard <- function(res, title, xmax = NULL) {
  d <- res |> mutate(competitor = fct_reorder(competitor, -test))
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(y = competitor)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = test - se, xmax = test + se), width = 0.25, colour = "grey60", orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(aes(x = test, shape = "test MSE, 2,000 new rows"), size = 4, colour = v_dark) +
    geom_point(aes(x = train, shape = "training MSE"), size = 3.5, colour = m_pink, stroke = 1.2) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("test MSE, 2,000 new rows" = 16, "training MSE" = 1), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "mean squared error", y = NULL, title = title) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(size = 16))
  if (!is.null(xmax)) g <- g + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, xmax))
  g
}
```

## Truth A: sparse linear, tall and then wide

::: {.notes}
Left, tall: n = 300, p = 10. Least squares and the lasso sit on the floor (dotted line, the noise variance, the smallest population MSE; a realized test MSE on 2,000 rows can sit a little below it); the additive fit and the two-unit network are close, each with many more parameters to estimate; the forest and the tree pay for a shape they do not need; k-NN in ten dimensions is last. Right, wide: n = 100, p = 200, the same truth. Least squares and the additive fit have no unique fit; the lasso alone stays near the floor; ridge, the forest and k-NN are near the mean's score; the two-unit network, with over 400 weights for 100 rows, fits the training rows exactly and is last. The hollow points: the forest's training error is a quarter of its test error; least squares' training error sits above its test error here (one realization; the theorem is about averages).
:::

```{r}
#| label: lb-A
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-width: 12
leaderboard(res_A, "tall: n = 300, p = 10") + leaderboard(res_Aw, "wide: n = 100, p = 200")
```

Dotted line: the noise variance, the smallest population MSE. For this sparse truth the lasso ties least squares when $n \gg p$, and alone stays near the floor when $p > n$

## Truth B: additive smooth

::: {.notes}
The additive fit near the floor, J = 3 chosen; the forest and least squares behind it, the tree further, k-NN last. The forest can bend, but it bends with rectangles and needs many of them for a smooth curve; the plane cannot bend at all. The curves were part 3's.
:::

```{r}
#| label: lb-B
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "75%"
leaderboard(res_B, "n = 300, p = 10; three smooth curves, added")
```

The additive fit was built for this truth. A forest can bend, with rectangles; a plane cannot bend at all

## Truth C: thresholds with an interaction

::: {.notes}
The tree of depth 2 is the truth, so it sits on the floor; the forest close behind. A sum of one-input functions can hold at most two thirds of this signal (each input's share) and the smooth splines hold less than that, so the additive fit and least squares are far from the floor. The network could represent this step but does not find it from 300 rows: it needs data. k-NN last again. The tree's training error sits above its test error: another one-realization exception.
:::

```{r}
#| label: lb-C
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "75%"
leaderboard(res_C, "n = 300, p = 10; one step, two inputs at once")
```

A sum of one-input functions can hold each input's share of this step, two thirds of the signal at best, and not the product. Two questions in a row hold all of it

## CTF competition: the seven on Spotify

::: {.notes}
The baselines slide asked whether a shape could beat both; this is the answer on the selection tracks, the knobs chosen there (the one-SE bars are the selection set's). The two-unit network 486, additive splines 490 and the forest 493 lead, within a standard error of each other; the tree 512; the lasso with genre 525; k-NN 528; least squares 541; the mean 581. The hollow points are the training scores: the forest's is 86. The vault stays shut: the seminar refits on training plus selection and opens it once. What these data have: a nonlinear year effect and loudness, which the plane cannot bend to, and little else the inputs can see.
:::

```{r}
#| label: spotify-six
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-width: 11
y_tr <- sp_train$track_popularity; y_se <- sp_sel$track_popularity
sc_sp <- function(name, pred_tr, pred_se)
  tibble(competitor = name, train = mse(y_tr, pred_tr), sel = mse(y_se, pred_se), se = se_loss(y_se, pred_se))
f_gen <- reformulate(c(feat, "genre"), "track_popularity")
lam_sp <- lasso_sp$lambda[which.min(apply(predict(lasso_sp, sp_Xse), 2, function(q) mse(y_se, q)))]
gam_sp <- function(J) reformulate(c(sprintf("ns(%s, df = %d)", feat, J), "genre"), "track_popularity")
Js_sp <- c(2, 3, 4, 6)
J_sp <- Js_sp[which.min(sapply(Js_sp, function(J) mse(y_se, predict(lm(gam_sp(J), sp_train), sp_sel))))]
fit_gam_sp <- lm(gam_sp(J_sp), sp_train)
ds_sp <- c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8)
d_sp <- ds_sp[which.min(sapply(ds_sp, function(d) mse(y_se, predict(rpart(f_gen, sp_train,
          control = rpart.control(maxdepth = d, cp = 0, minbucket = 10)), sp_sel))))]
fit_tree_sp <- rpart(f_gen, sp_train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = d_sp, cp = 0, minbucket = 10))
fit_rf_sp <- randomForest(f_gen, sp_train, ntree = 300)
Ms_sp <- c(2, 4, 8, 16)
nn_sp <- function(X, y, M) { set.seed(10); nnet(X, y, size = M, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, maxit = 300, trace = FALSE) }
M_sp <- Ms_sp[which.min(sapply(Ms_sp, function(M) mse(y_se, predict(nn_sp(sp_Xtr, y_tr, M), sp_Xse))))]
fit_nn_sp <- nn_sp(sp_Xtr, y_tr, M_sp)
six <- bind_rows(
  sc_sp("the training mean", rep(mean(y_tr), length(y_tr)), rep(mean(y_tr), length(y_se))),
  sc_sp("least squares, 11 numeric inputs", fitted(fit_ls), predict(fit_ls, sp_sel)),
  sc_sp(paste0("k-NN, same inputs, k = ", k_sp), knn_predict(X_tr, X_tr, y_tr, k_sp), knn_predict(X_se, X_tr, y_tr, k_sp)),
  sc_sp("lasso, + genre", predict(lasso_sp, sp_Xtr, s = lam_sp), predict(lasso_sp, sp_Xse, s = lam_sp)),
  sc_sp(paste0("additive splines, + genre, J = ", J_sp), fitted(fit_gam_sp), predict(fit_gam_sp, sp_sel)),
  sc_sp(paste0("tree, + genre, depth ", d_sp), predict(fit_tree_sp, sp_train), predict(fit_tree_sp, sp_sel)),
  sc_sp("forest, + genre, defaults", predict(fit_rf_sp, sp_train), predict(fit_rf_sp, sp_sel)),
  sc_sp(paste0("network, + genre, M = ", M_sp), predict(fit_nn_sp, sp_Xtr), predict(fit_nn_sp, sp_Xse))) |>
  mutate(competitor = fct_reorder(competitor, -sel))
ggplot(six, aes(y = competitor)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = sel - se, xmax = sel + se), width = 0.25, colour = "grey60", orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(aes(x = sel, shape = "selection MSE, 2,000 tracks"), size = 4, colour = v_dark) +
  geom_point(aes(x = train, shape = "training MSE"), size = 3.5, colour = m_pink, stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("selection MSE, 2,000 tracks" = 16, "training MSE" = 1), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "mean squared error", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Knobs chosen on the selection tracks, scored there. The three that can bend beat the plane by about four standard errors and are within one of each other; the forest's training score is `r round(six$train[six$competitor == "forest, + genre, defaults"])`. The vault stays shut: the seminar refits and opens it once

## Four dimensions, not one {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Four questions about the world, not one scale from simple to complex: a truth can be tall and interactive, or wide and smooth. Each family is a bet on an answer; week 4's no free lunch says the bet is doing the work, and the selection set says which bet paid on these data (Spotify: smooth in year and loudness, roughly additive, so the splines, the forest and a two-unit network). k-NN lost on every simulated truth: ten inputs, 300 points, week 1's curse with a price on it. Week 7 puts a rate on that price.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.97em"}
| Axis | The question about $f^\star$ | Who bets which way |
|---|---|---|
| **wide or tall** | how $p$ compares with $n$ | least squares, the additive fit and a network need $n \gg$ their parameters; ridge and the lasso fit at any $p$ |
| **sparse or dense** | how many inputs matter | the lasso bets few; least squares and ridge spread the fit over all; a forest tolerates idle inputs, $k$-NN pays for them |
| **smooth or discontinuous** | how $f^\star$ moves with each input | splines, $k$-NN and networks bet smooth; trees bet on steps |
| **additive or interactive** | whether inputs act separately | the additive fit bets separately; trees, forests, $k$-NN and networks allow interactions |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,30,48]"}
:::

Four separate questions, not one scale from simple to complex. A family is a bet on the answers; a selection set says which bet paid on these data

::: {.retrieval}
Week 1's curse: $k$-NN lost on every truth, ten inputs and 300 points. Week 4's no free lunch: no family won every truth, and none can.
:::

## What the training error hides {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes for the ask; collect two orderings before the reveal. Why anyone cared: the training error is the only error you can compute without new data. The hollow points sat left of the filled ones on most rows, the forest's by a factor of four, and right of them on a few (least squares on truth A, the tree on truth C); the question is whether the usual direction is a law, and what the exceptions are. Expected answer after the theorem: it is a statement about averages over training sets, and one realization of 300 rows can go either way by a little; the test MSE is itself a noisy number. Week 4's symbols: a class, the best in it, what the data return.
:::

On most rows of the leaderboards the training MSE sat below the test or selection MSE, the forest's by a factor of four on the truths and of six on Spotify; on a few rows it sat above. Luck, or a law, and what are the exceptions?

Training data $(x_i, y_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, independent draws from the population; a class $\mathcal F$ fixed before the data (the planes; the spline fits with a given basis); $f_{\mathcal F}$ the best in $\mathcal F$, the minimizer of $R$ over it; $\hat f$ the empirical risk minimizer, the minimizer of $\hat R_n$ over $\mathcal F$ (week 4)

::: {.ask}
Three numbers: $\mathbb E[\hat R_n(\hat f)]$, $R(f_{\mathcal F})$, $\mathbb E[R(\hat f)]$. Put them in order, and write down what you used to do it.
:::

## Optimism theorem {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Stated; the three-line proof is exercise 1. The heuristic first: f-hat was chosen to make the training losses small, so it beats any fixed member of the class on the training data, and a fixed member's training error is unbiased for its risk (the one line that uses the sampling assumption); on the population f-hat cannot beat the best member. Chain the three. Covered: least squares, and a spline basis whose knots are fixed in advance (ns() places them at sample quantiles, so strictly the class depends on the data). Ridge and the lasso in their constrained form with a fixed radius t are minimizers over a fixed class; at a fixed lambda they are not (noiseless Y = X: ridge has positive training error while the best line has risk zero, so the left inequality fails). Not covered: a tree (greedy), a forest, k-NN, a network as fitted (gradient descent returns a local minimum, not the minimizer), and any knob chosen on the data. The direction was the usual one on the leaderboards, with exceptions, but the theorem is about the minimizer and about averages.
:::

A function fixed before the data has an unbiased training error; $\hat f$ was chosen to make its own small, and cannot beat $f_{\mathcal F}$ on the population

Training data i.i.d.; $\mathcal F$ fixed before the data; $\hat f$ the empirical risk minimizer over $\mathcal F$; $f_{\mathcal F}$ the best in $\mathcal F$ (risks finite, minimizers exist). Then
$$
\mathbb E\big[\hat R_n(\hat f)\big] \;\le\; R(f_{\mathcal F}) \;\le\; \mathbb E\big[R(\hat f)\big]
$$

::: {.leave}
Training error flatters the model: on average it sits below the best risk the class can reach, and the fitted model's risk above it. A test set estimates $R(\hat f)$; its average is the right end.
:::

**Proof**: exercise 1. Covers least squares, a fixed spline basis, ridge and lasso with a fixed radius; not a fixed $\lambda$, a tree, a forest, $k$-NN, or a knob chosen on the data

A plane, a sparse plane, a sum of curves, a set of rectangles, an average of many, a composition. Four questions about the world decide which bet pays

#### The protocol decides what you may believe

Fit on the training rows, choose on the selection rows, open the test set once

On average, for every class and every minimizer. *How much flexibility to allow, and how to choose it: week 7*
